answers.answer: The client contacts the service entry point, the reverse proxy selects and forwards to a backend, that backend performs the operation, and its response returns through the balancer to the client. Choose L7 for /search versus /purchase pools: it must read HTTP contents, so an HTTPS proxy normally terminates client TLS; backend encryption is a separate choice. L4 typically selects a backend per TCP connection using network information, so all requests reusing that connection can reach the same backend without fresh selection. One adequate server may suffice when neither distribution nor redundant serving is needed.

evidence.quote: The balancer forwards the request to a selected backend, which performs the operation and returns a response through the balancer to the client.
Path routing requires readable HTTP contents.
Many HTTP requests can reuse that connection. They can all reach the same backend; adding requests on that connection does not force new selections.
One adequate server may be enough if the service does not need traffic distribution or redundant serving.

answers.answer: Round robin takes turns among eligible backends and is simple for similar servers/work, but a cheap lookup and long request each count once, so equal turns do not ensure equal work. Least connections prefers fewer active connections and may help with varying durations, but one connection may hide much more work. Weights control traffic share; twice measured capacity suggests starting at twice the weight, but configured weights are neither live measurements nor guarantees. Measure latency and resources to decide. Adding an API backend cannot remove a saturated shared database bottleneck. Availability after failure requires a reachable alternate entry path through managed availability or redundant frontends with working, tested failover, plus enough spare capacity on survivors for redirected load; visibly limit or reject excess work if capacity is insufficient.

evidence.quote: a quick read and a slow report still each count as one request.
Prefers the backend with fewer active connections.
one connection may carry far more work than another.
A server with twice the measured capacity might start with twice the weight. Configured weights are not a live measurement or a performance guarantee.
they do not remove a saturated shared database bottleneck.
After one backend fails, the survivors need enough capacity for the remaining load.
Use an available managed entry or redundant frontends with working failover, and test that path.

answers.answer: A 200 health response proves only the probed capability: it does not show the purchase handler can access its required database. A readiness check should reflect capabilities needed for useful application work. Even improved checks have limited coverage, periodic intervals, and failure thresholds; failure can occur immediately after a pass, so detection takes time. Once detected and removed from eligibility, the backend stops receiving new selections. This cannot complete, undo, or safely replay already underway requests, which can still fail. The product's all-unhealthy policy also needs checking, since some send traffic to unhealthy targets when every check fails.

evidence.quote: Readiness means it can accept useful new work: a process can answer /health while an application handler cannot reach its required database.
Checks have limited coverage, intervals and failure thresholds; a backend can fail just after passing. Detection takes time.
Once detected and removed from eligible backends, it stops receiving new selections. Requests already underway can still fail; removal does not complete, undo or safely replay them.
Some balancers send traffic to unhealthy targets when every target fails its checks, rather than refusing all traffic.

answers.answer: B cannot read a cart stored only in A's memory, and losing A can lose the cart's only copy. Stickiness prefers A for this user's requests, helping ordinary access while A works, but it can skew load and restrict placement. It neither copies the cart nor preserves it if A fails. Shared session storage lets either backend read the cart, at the cost of access or coordination work and a shared dependency whose availability matters.

evidence.quote: If a server keeps a user's session only in A's memory, B cannot read it. Losing A can lose the only copy.
It can keep ordinary requests on A, but skew load and restrict placement. It does not copy the session or preserve it when A fails.
Lets either backend read the session. It adds access or coordination work and a shared dependency whose availability matters too.

answers.answer: Stop new assignments to A, manage existing connection lifetimes or stop accepting further requests, and track accepted work while allowing it to finish within a bounded deadline. The accepted 20-second request is in-flight work rather than a new assignment: allow it to finish if the deadline permits, then shut down once accepted work completes or the deadline expires. At expiry, forced termination may interrupt unfinished work; it is not automatically moved to B. L4 assigns connections, and the reused connection can carry more HTTP requests even after new connections are stopped. Therefore draining must address existing connections and further request acceptance as well as new connection assignments; L7 request-aware draining still must track already accepted requests.

evidence.quote: During a deployment, draining stops new assignments to A while allowing in-flight work, meaning requests already underway, to finish within a deadline. Shut A down after completion or when that deadline expires.

Stopping new L4 connections does not stop new HTTP requests on existing connections. A drain must also manage those connection lifetimes or stop accepting further requests. L7 request-aware draining must still track already accepted work.
Forced termination at the deadline may interrupt unfinished requests. Their work is not automatically moved to B.

answers.answer: The purchase may remain committed even though its response never arrives, so timeout does not tell the client whether the effect happened. A blind retry on B may purchase again. Give one logical purchase a stable idempotency key reused for all attempts, and have all backends use a shared durable key-and-result record. In one database transaction uniquely reserve the key, apply the purchase effect, and record the result, committing all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without applying the purchase again. Separate check-then-write operations can race or leave a crash gap. A fresh key disguises a retry as another operation, and A-only memory cannot reliably protect a retry on B. Bound attempts and delay them because extra requests consume capacity and can worsen overload; retries do not replace duplicate protection or guarantee success. No gaps identified in the supplied lesson for these questions.

evidence.quote: A backend commits a write, but its response is lost. The client cannot tell whether the write completed. A blind retry on another backend can repeat the effect.
A stable ID for one logical operation, reused on every attempt.

All backends use a shared durable record of the key and result. In one database transaction, reserve the key uniquely, apply the effect and record the result; commit all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without applying the effect again. Separate check-then-write steps can race or leave a crash gap.
A new key per retry, or a key remembered only in one server's memory, cannot reliably protect retries elsewhere.
Bound retry attempts and delay them: extra requests consume capacity and can deepen overload.
